# Deep behavioural pass — modulation, music and custom components

My half of the second QA pass. The first one was rejected as too shallow and that was the right
call: it proved that properties can be written and that controls mount, and called that coverage.
Neither is behaviour.

**This ledger is generated by the run, not written by hand.** `browser-checks/behaviourKit.mjs`
carries a `Ledger` whose `check()` both asserts and records, so a row cannot say "verified" unless
an assertion ran and passed. The tables print at the end of every check; the counts below are from
the runs at the commit this document belongs to.

---

## What counts as evidence here

A property is **verified** when its declared promise was turned into an exact expected result, and
that result was measured off one of:

- the rendered SVG as structure — every shape with its numeric attributes and the paint that
  actually resolved (`geo()`), or the positioned divs for the renderers that use them (`dom()`);
- a **rasterised pixel** — the SVG serialised, drawn into a canvas, and read back, because a fill
  attribute is what was asked for and a pixel is what happened;
- the **fan-out values** a bound device parameter would receive (`ports()`);
- the **note funnel** — the actual note-on/off, channel and velocity the panel played;
- a **real pointer gesture** through the app.

…and then again after the panel was serialised to its on-disk `.cepanel` format, parsed back and
**reopened as a panel** (`reopen()`), so the second measurement goes through a renderer that has
never seen the original.

Explicitly **not** evidence, and not counted as any: that a property could be written, that the
control mounted, that `innerHTML` changed, or that a model round-trip preserved a value without a
renderer ever reading it.

## D-1 — `DrumPads.velocityFrom: 'centre'` ignores the horizontal axis

**Fixed.** `PanelPreviewSurface.svelte`, the drum strike path.

`'centre'` is a declared value (`PAD_VELOCITY_SOURCES`) and is settable from every scripting
language (`componentTables.js` maps `drumpads.velocityFrom` to that table, and all seven engines
expose it). Its rule, and the comment defending it, are explicit:

> 'centre' measures the CHEBYSHEV distance to the middle — the larger of the two axis distances —
> rather than the euclidean one, because a pad is a square and a ring of equal response should
> follow its edges. With euclidean distance the corners are further from the middle than the edge
> midpoints are, so a corner strike would come out quieter than a rim strike beside it, which is
> backwards from how a square pad feels under a hand.

That entire argument is about two axes. Only one was working.

**Measured**, velocity 100, a strike at each position:

| Strike | Expected | Measured (before) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dead centre | 77 | 77 |
| near the top edge | 27 | 27 |
| near the right edge | 24 | **77** |
| the corner | 24 | **77** |

**Cause.** `drumStrike` computes `const base = strikeVelocity(control, hit.strikeY, hit.strikeX)`
correctly — with both axes. Every corner branch passes `base` on to `drumHit`. The plain-hit branch
did not, and `drumHit` then worked the velocity out itself by calling
`strikeVelocity(control, strikeY)` with no third argument, so `strikeX` fell back to its default of
`0.5` and `dx` was always zero. The Chebyshev maximum collapsed to the vertical axis alone.

Note the direction of the failure: the corner — the exact case the rule exists for — came out at
**full** velocity rather than quiet, so a test that only moved up and down the pad would pass.

**Fix.** One line: the default branch passes the `base` it already has. Roll behaviour is unchanged
(`drumHit` reads `opts?.roll === true`, so an absent flag is the same `false` as an absent `opts`).

**Regression.** `behaviourNotes.mjs` asserts the middle, both axes separately, corner-equals-edge,
and left-right symmetry. Reverting the fix fails with `expected: 24, measured: 77`.

## D-2 — `DrumPads.map: 'chromatic'` showed GM drum names, not pitches

**Fixed.** `utils/drumPadLayout.js`.

The properties panel's own hint reads **"Chromatic = labelled by pitch."** On the default grid it
was labelled by drum: Kick, Stick, Snare, Clap.

**Cause.** `resolveDrumPads` built the chromatic label with `drumNoteLabel(note, true)`, and that
helper prefers the General MIDI name whenever one exists — which is every note from **35 to 81**,
i.e. the whole range a drum grid uses. So `chromatic` and `gm` produced identical labels everywhere
a user would ever see them, and differed only in choke groups.

**Fix.** A new `drumPitchLabel(note)` that answers the pitch question directly, used by the
chromatic branch. `drumNoteLabel` is untouched, so the GM map and the long `fullName` are unchanged.

**The existing unit test already knew.** `test/drumPadLayout.test.js` carried this pair:

```js
// a chromatic pad on a GM note still reads as a pitch, not as a drum
assert.equal(drumPads(dp({ map: 'chromatic', … baseNote: 36 }))[0].label, 'Kick');
```

The comment states the rule correctly and the assertion beneath it pins the opposite. The
expectation had been written down from the output rather than from the rule immediately above it —
which is the same failure mode as the pass this document replaces, one line apart. The assertion now
matches its comment, and a second one pins that GM still names the kit.

## D-3 — pressing a control scrolled the canvas out from under the pointer

**Fixed.** `PanelPreviewSurface.svelte`, the generic pointer-down handler (one argument).

This one is surface-wide rather than mine alone, and it is the reason it is worth writing up
carefully: it silently displaced **every** absolute-positioning gesture in preview, on every control
type, by an amount that depended on where the control happened to sit.

**Symptom.** Dragging an Orbit satellite to a point due east of its own drawn hub committed an angle
of **−12.9°** instead of 0°. Consistently, to fifteen decimal places, across three different ways of
computing the target — which is what made it clear the target was not the variable.

**Measured.** Tracing the control's own `getBoundingClientRect()` through the gesture:

```
pointerdown   rect.top 477   panel-surface scrollTop 0
pointermove   rect.top 455   panel-surface scrollTop 22
```

The control moves **22px up between the press and the first move**. Suppressing the scroll and
sweeping the drop point gives a clean, exact mapping with no offset at all:

```
dy = -24  →  +14.04°      dy =  0  →   0.00°
dy = -10  →   +5.95°      dy = +10 →  −5.95°
```

**Cause.** The pointer-down handler called `event.currentTarget?.focus?.()`. Focusing an element the
browser considers less than fully visible makes it scroll that element into view — here, on
pointer-down, *while the pointer is already on it*. The control slides away under the finger and
everything that positions absolutely from the pointer lands short by the scroll distance.

**Fix.** `focus({ preventScroll: true })`, on the pointer path only. The five keyboard handlers keep
the plain `focus()`: scrolling a control into view is the right thing when you arrived by Tab rather
than by pointing at something already on screen.

**Why the earlier checks missed it.** It is position-dependent. The Envelope in `behaviourCurves`
asserts exact drop coordinates and passes — that control sat where no scroll was needed. A component
whose check only asks "did anything change?" would never see it at all.

Root independently observed the same canvas jump from the other side of the codebase.

## Rows that are not "verified", stated plainly

**Inert — declared, and read by nothing:**

- `Envelope.xLabel`, `Envelope.yLabel`. No reader in `CE/src`, `CE/web/src`, `tools/` or the script
  API; `EnvelopeRenderer` draws no `<text>` at all. Written only by
  `tools/scripts/an1x-panel/make-an1x-panel.mjs`. Not reachable from the properties panel either, so
  there is no user-visible symptom — which is why this is recorded rather than fixed.
  (`timeMax` and `timeUnit` sit beside them in the same comment block and are **not** inert: both
  drive the Envelope Designer's stage readout via `designerModel.envelopeStages`, and `timeMax` is
  scriptable. Verified.)

**Unverified — nothing in this environment can observe it:**

- `Envelope.phaseSourceId`, `Router.sourceControlId` — need a second control driving them live.
- `Router.inputChannel`, `Router.polyMode` — need inbound MIDI, including polyphonic aftertouch.
- `DrumPads.echo` / `echoChannel` / `echoColour` — need an inbound MIDI route.
- `DrumPads.rollRate` / `rollSync` — need a running transport to sync against. The free-running
  `rollHz` path *is* verified (20 Hz over 400 ms, with `rollVelocity` confirmed as an accent
  followed by quieter repeats, and `rollDelay` holding the first repeat back).
- `Orbit.syncToTransport` / `cycleBars`, `Turing.syncToTransport` / `division` — same reason.
- `Orbit.showTrails` — the trail only exists while the clock runs, so its shape is a moving target.

**Environment, not product:** `browser-checks/screenDock.mjs` cannot run here — it launches
`channel: 'msedge'`, which is Windows-only. Everything else in the existing browser suite passes
with these changes, with no assertion failures.

## Harness mistakes made and corrected, so they are not repeated

Every one of these produced a green-looking or red-looking result that was about the test, not the
product. They are listed because the previous pass's real failure was not noticing this class.

1. **Counting the sustain marker as a grid line.** Dashed lines are markers; the grid has no dash.
2. **`pad = 3`** guessed for the Matrix cell inset. It is `min(4, 14% of each side)`, and the guess
   passed on tolerance — which is worse than failing, because it then stops catching anything.
3. **Matrix port keys.** The section comment says a cell is a port `"Src → Dest"`; that is the
   *label*. The id is `cell_r_c`. Both are now asserted, including that renaming a row renames the
   label and keeps the id, so an existing binding survives a rename.
4. **`rect[rx="6"]` is also the drum header**, and `circle[0]` of a Router is the source-chip dot,
   not a curve node. A selector is an assumption about markup until it is checked against the
   renderer that writes it.
5. **A width test for the drum header** silently returned an empty grid on a 1×1 layout. Height is
   the discriminator.
6. **Striking "rect number n" to test `origin`.** `origin` does not reorder the DOM — it decides
   which pad each screen cell belongs to. Position is the only way to measure it.
7. **Toggle state leaking between scenarios**: a pad still latched from the previous block gave a
   note-off that read as a choke.
8. **Two panels share control ids after a reopen.** `deserializePanel` preserves them, so a lookup
   across all panels returns the copy that is *not* on screen — reading the old control while
   dragging the new one. The kit now resolves from the active panel. (The application itself is
   right here: `applyControlPatchesById` scopes writes to the active panel by design.)
9. **Comparing live session state across a reopen.** The drum header's right-hand slot shows either
   the last pad hit or the channel. A reopened panel has correctly never been hit; asserting
   otherwise would demand that a saved file remember a keypress.
10. **`kit.click()` holds for 40 ms**, which outlived a 40 ms one-shot gate and read as "the gate did
    not hold".
11. **Reading live state out of the document.** Twice: the Orbit's run clock injects `__phase` into
    the *resolved* control rather than writing a phase into the document sixty times a second, and
    the Turing's randomness mutates the *preview session* because preview is a rehearsal that leaves
    the saved panel alone. Both read as "the clock is stopped". The fix was to measure the drawing
    and the session — and, for the Turing, to add the assertion that actually matters: that all that
    churning leaves the document untouched.
12. **Parking a Timbre puck exactly on an anchor**, so the press grabbed the anchor — a different and
    equally real gesture — and the puck never moved.
13. **SVG coordinates plus the control's screen origin.** The svg is not necessarily flush with its
    control element; adding the two offsets every target by that gap.
